metaDescription: Concise explanations of all the financial metrics and terms that appear in AI Stock Analyzer.
title: Finance glossary
intro: Concise explanations of all the financial terms that appear in AI Stock Analyzer. Linkable via anchor, e.g. /glossary#sharpe-ratio.

aktie.description: Ownership interest in a company. The holder is a part-owner with voting rights (for common shares) and a claim on profit distributions (dividends).

beta.description: Measure of price movement relative to the overall market. Beta 1 means moves in lock-step with the market, 0.5 half as much, 2.0 twice as much. Estimated by regression on historical returns.

book-value.description: Shareholders' equity on the balance sheet divided by shares outstanding. The basis for the price-to-book ratio.

cagr.description: Average annual growth rate computed from a start and end value over N years. Formula: (end / start)^(1/N) − 1.

conviction-score.description: Our own 0–100 score that combines analyst consensus, valuation, 52-week position, AI recommendation and momentum into a single conviction reading. 75+ = strong conviction.

cvar.description: Expected loss on the days when VaR is exceeded — in other words the average loss in the worst tail. Stricter than VaR.

dcf.description: Valuation method that discounts future free cash flows back to today's value. Key inputs: growth rate, terminal growth, WACC. Small changes in WACC and terminal growth have large effects — always sensitivity-check.

dividendenrendite.description: Dividend per share divided by price. A high yield can be attractive — or a warning sign because the price has fallen sharply and the payout may be at risk.

drawdown.description: Decline from the last high to the current price (or the trough before a recovery), expressed as a percentage. Max drawdown is the largest drop observed historically.

ebit.description: Profit before interest and taxes. Reflects operating profitability independent of the capital structure.

ebitda.short: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, Amortization
ebitda.description: EBIT plus depreciation and amortisation. An approximation of operating cash flow, but ignores CapEx and working-capital effects — treat with care.

eps.description: Net income divided by shares outstanding. The denominator behind the P/E ratio.

fcf.description: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditures (CapEx). The cash actually available for dividends, buybacks or debt repayment.

faktor-exposure.description: Decomposition of a portfolio into typical style factors: Value, Growth, Size (large/small cap), Quality, Momentum. Reveals which style currently dominates — even in seemingly diversified portfolios.

forward-pe.description: Current price divided by expected earnings for the next 12 months. Reacts to estimate revisions faster than the trailing P/E.

gordon-growth.description: Formula for the terminal value in a DCF: TV = FCF × (1 + g) / (WACC − g). Only makes sense when WACC > g.

growth.description: Companies with above-average revenue or earnings growth, usually at a higher valuation. The opposite of value.

kgv.description: Current price divided by annual earnings per share. P/E 15 means you're paying for 15 years of current earnings. A high number can mean expensive — or high growth expectations.

kbv.description: Price divided by book value per share. More informative than P/E for capital-intensive, balance-sheet-heavy companies such as banks and insurers.

monte-carlo.description: Stochastic method that simulates many future paths (e.g. 1,000 paths over 1 year). Result: a distribution of possible outcomes with percentiles. We use a historical bootstrap (randomly drawing observed daily returns) rather than a normal distribution — more robust to fat tails.

momentum.description: A factor based on the idea that stocks which have risen over the past 6–12 months tend to keep rising. As a simplification the 52-week position shows how far a price is below or above its 52-week low / high.

net-debt.description: Total debt minus cash and short-term securities. Important when converting enterprise value to equity value.

payout-ratio.description: Share of net income paid out as a dividend. Below 60% is considered sustainable; above 100% means the dividend is funded out of substance — a warning sign.

peer-compare.description: Side-by-side comparison of several companies in the same sector across fundamental and technical metrics. Helps surface outliers.

portfolio-health.description: Overall grade A–F derived from five weighted sub-scores: diversification, quality, valuation, momentum and risk. Transparent and decomposable — no black box.

quality.description: Style factor that rewards high margins, stable profitability and solid balance sheets. In AI Stock Analyzer it is derived from operating margin, profit margin and debt/equity.

rebalance.description: Restoring target weights in a portfolio by buying underweight and selling overweight positions. Imposes discipline against concentration.

reverse-dcf.description: Inverts the DCF: instead of computing a fair value, you ask which growth rate the market is currently pricing in. An excellent tool for making expectations tangible.

roe.description: Net income divided by shareholders' equity. 15%+ is generally considered solid, above 25% very high — but watch out for high leverage, which inflates ROE artificially.

sharpe-ratio.description: Excess return over the risk-free rate divided by the standard deviation of returns. Measures risk-adjusted performance — higher is better, 1+ is considered good.

short-interest.description: Number of shares sold short as a fraction of the free float. A high short interest can trigger a short squeeze on positive news.

size.description: Style factor for company size. Large caps (> 10 bn) offer stability, small caps (< 2 bn) historically deliver higher returns at higher volatility.

sortino-ratio.description: Like the Sharpe ratio, but the denominator uses only downside volatility. Penalises only negative moves, not positive ones — arguably more economically meaningful.

stress-test.description: Applies historical crisis periods (COVID 2020, financial crisis 2008, etc.) to today's portfolio. Shows how much it would have lost if the same crisis were to occur today.

twr.description: Return calculation that neutralises the impact of deposits and withdrawals. Used for fair performance comparisons between portfolios with different cash flows.

value.description: Companies trading at low valuations (low P/E, P/B), usually with slower growth. Historically value has delivered a modest long-term premium.

var.description: A statistical loss that will not be exceeded with a given probability (typically 95% or 99%) over a horizon. Empirically from historical returns or parametrically under a normal assumption — both have limits.

vix.description: The “fear index” — implied 30-day volatility of the S&P 500, derived from option prices. Below 15 = calm, above 30 = panic. Historically contrarian: VIX spikes often mark local price bottoms.

volatilitaet.description: Standard deviation of returns, usually annualised. High = strong swings. Widely used as a risk measure but incomplete because it treats upside and downside symmetrically.

wacc.description: Weighted average of equity and debt costs. The discount rate in a DCF. Typically 6–12% depending on industry and leverage. Higher WACC → lower fair value.

yield-curve.description: Government bond yields plotted by maturity. Normally upward-sloping (longer maturities = higher yield). An inverted curve (short > long) has historically been a recession leading indicator with a 12–18 month lead.

hhi.description: Sum of squared weights in a portfolio. 1.0 = everything in a single position, near 0 = broadly diversified. A good gauge of concentration risk.
